stories.title: Jio IPO closes today: retail is oversubscribed now, so it's a lottery for about 70 lakh winning slips
stories.label: HOT
stories.window: Today, Fri 23 Oct (bidding closes; UPI mandates by evening) to Mon 26 Oct (allotment). Listing Wed 28 Oct is the turn after that. Final subscription and application counts come out tonight.
happening: New since yesterday: the retail line filled. On day 1 retail closed at about 0.73×; on day 2 it was fully subscribed by about 11 am, two hours into bidding (ETV Bharat, BSE data), and at 1.55× by 5:54 pm (Chittorgarh). Overall 5.40×; QIB 12.87×; NII 5.67×; employees 2.05× (Chittorgarh, 22 Oct, 5:54 pm).

Because retail is now oversubscribed, allotment is by lottery: each winning application gets one minimum lot of 12 shares (₹13,428 at the top of the band), so 14 lots and 1 lot have about the same chance (SEBI ICDR rule, as several creators explain it).

The retail quota is 8,50,37,326 shares (Chittorgarh). Divided into lots of 12, that is about 70.86 lakh winning slips at most (our arithmetic; a YouTube Short gives the same figure). The number of applications, published after the close, decides the odds.
Day 1 overall was 3.20×, booked in 100 minutes; bids of about ₹69,800 crore for 62.36 crore shares by 5 pm on day 1 (ETV Bharat).

The issue: ₹30,213 crore, 27 crore fresh shares, band ₹1,065–1,119, valuation about $108.3 billion; anchor book about ₹8,110 crore from 212 anchors, bids over ₹2.5 lakh crore (ETV Bharat). P/E at the top of the band 33.31× against a peer average of 22.35× (Business Today).
Dates: closes 23 Oct; allotment 26 Oct; refunds and demat credit 27 Oct; listing 28 Oct (IPOPremium; earlier desk sources).
curiosity_gaps: India's biggest IPO now has more retail applicants than slips. How many people applied for about 70 lakh winning slips, and what are your real odds?
Somebody put ₹1.88 lakh into 14 lots; somebody else put ₹13,428 into one. On Monday they have the same chance. Why does the bigger cheque buy nothing?
On day 1 the public stayed away while the funds bid 9×. On day 2 the public piled in. What changed overnight?

stories.title: Oil at $112 and everything fell on the same day: shares, gold and silver; ₹3.84 lakh crore gone on Thursday, Nifty down 13.5% this year
stories.label: HOT
stories.window: Fri 23 Oct to about Thu 29 Oct. Next turns: the US Fed meeting on 27–28 Oct, crude, and any pump-price hike by the state oil companies.
happening: Thu 22 Oct: Sensex −460.30 to 73,249.39, Nifty −123.70 to 22,687.65, a third straight fall; BSE-listed companies lost about ₹3,83,881 crore of value in the day (Free Press Journal; Business Standard).
Breadth: 226 stocks hit their lower circuit and nearly 400 hit 52-week lows; October's advance-decline ratio is the lowest since March (Business Today).
The year: the Nifty is down 13.53% in 2026 and 3% in the past month; Midcap 100 and Smallcap 100 both down 8% in a month (Business Today).

The same day, the usual shelters fell too: MCX silver −₹8,593 to ₹2,00,575/kg, a seven-month low, down 10% in October; MCX gold −₹2,300 to ₹1,43,600 per 10 g, a two-month low (Business Today, 22 Oct, 9:39 pm).

Why: Brent up 2.78% to $111.85 on attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi strikes on Saudi targets; higher oil means fear of inflation and higher interest rates, and gold and silver pay no interest (Business Today). DBS sees Indian inflation near 6% this quarter and leaves room for another RBI hike in December (Business Today). The RBI already raised its rate to 5.50% on 7 Oct (The Core).

Private pumps have already moved: Jio-bp raised petrol ₹5 and diesel ₹3 a litre from 11 Oct; Nayara the same from 3 Oct (Goodreturns; Sarkaritel). State-run companies haven't (Business Today headline, 21 Oct).
curiosity_gaps: Gold and silver are meant to rise when shares fall. On Thursday all three fell together. What does oil at $112 have to do with your silver?
₹3.84 lakh crore went in one day, the Nifty is down 13.5% this year, and yet most people's SIPs haven't stopped. Who is selling?
Two weeks before Dhanteras, silver is down 10% this month. Is cheaper silver good news or a warning?

stories.title: India has frozen new SIPs into gold funds, the eighth step this year to protect the rupee, and the playbook is 2013's
stories.label: FLAT
stories.window: Fri 23 Oct to Fri 6 Nov (Dhanteras). Later turns: October gold-import data in mid-November, and whenever 'until further notice' ends.
happening: New since we sent it on 16 Oct: The Core (23 Oct) lays the freeze out as the eighth step this year to defend the rupee, and compares it with 2013.

The freeze: from 16 Oct, fund houses stopped lump sums, switch-ins, new SIPs and SIP top-ups in gold funds of funds; 17 fund houses, 20 schemes by Friday (Cofacto's count). Existing SIPs and redemptions continue 'until further notice'. Shriram MF says the instruction came from SEBI through AMFI, unpublished; Reuters says it followed talks with SEBI to shield the rupee (The Core).

The eight steps: RBI sold a net $9.76 billion in March; on 10 May the Prime Minister asked Indians not to buy gold for weddings for a year; on 13 May the duty on gold and silver went from 6% to 15%; silver bar imports needed a licence from 16 May; in June direct gold-ETF subscriptions over ₹25 crore were stopped; RBI dollar-deposit swaps from 8 June; a repo hike to 5.50% on 7 Oct; the gold-fund freeze on 16 Oct (The Core).
Why: reserves fell from a record $785.7 billion on 4 Sept to $734.6 billion on 2 Oct, about $50 billion in four weeks; the rupee hit a record low of 96.82 to the dollar in May (The Core).
Savers kept buying gold on paper: gold-ETF inflows ₹1,559 crore in July, ₹2,597 crore in August, ₹4,450.61 crore in September (The Core).

2013: duty raised, the finance minister asked Indians to buy less gold, and Reliance Mutual Fund suspended its gold savings fund until the rupee steadied; this year's swap drawdown is about four times 2013's $34 billion (The Core).
curiosity_gaps: Your gold SIP is allowed, but you can't start a new one. Why does the government care whether you buy gold on paper?
The Prime Minister asked people not to buy wedding gold, duty went from 6% to 15%, and now the funds are shut. What is India running short of?
It happened once before, in 2013, and the fund reopened when the rupee steadied. What did the people who kept buying gold then end up with?
